Conclusions:
1. In accordance with reference (b) the Initiating Event (or first unwanted outcome) for this casualty was
Mr. Staples' fall overboard from the port paddlewheel support arm in the area between the aftermost
vessel bulkhead and the paddlewheel.
2. The causal factors that led to the fall overboard are as follows:
a) Environment: Although the weather at the time of the incident was relatively benign, the river
current speed at the vessel's position in the Columbia River was around 4 knots. Not only did the
strong river current cause the paddlewheel to turn in a slow, forward-moving direction,
unbalancing Mr. Staples, but it carried him swiftly away from the vessel once he had entered the
water. Every minute that Mr. Staples was in the river, he drifted an additional 125 yards from the
vessel. Witnesses indicated that they lost sight of him within just a couple of minutes, and by the
time the rescue boat was in the water, he was likely half-a-mile downstream.
b)
Organizational Factors: There are three organizational factors that involve American Cruise
Lines, Inc. policies and procedures.
1) Life Jacket Policy: American Cruise Lines, Inc. does not have a policy with respect to
life jacket use for personnel working in dangerous areas of the main deck. The majority
of the P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST's main deck was surrounded by 39 ½ inch high
railings with three additional courses to protect passengers and crew. The most
dangerous, and least protected, area of the vessel's main deck is the stern. Captain
stated that the life jacket policy was only for engineers working on the
machinery or the paddlewheel on the stern. Crewmembers handling lines, or anyone else,
in the vicinity are not required by policy to wear them. An effective life jacket policy,
enforced by the ship's management, would stress the importance of wearing life jackets
any time that crewmembers are working in dangerous areas of the vessel, and may have
given Mr. Staples good cause for putting on a life jacket prior to approaching the stern.
2) Station Bill: The P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST's Station Bill does not identify a person
to throw the "Man Overboard" life ring. As a consequence, a lighted life ring was not
thrown until the vessel was directed by the Coast Guard helicopter around an hour later.
Had the Station Bill indicated that a certain crewmember throw the life ring, it would
have been done much sooner (probably within a minute or two), and may have given Mr.
Staples something to hold for buoyancy while the rescue boat was launched to recover
him.
3) Authorized Personnel: Neither the American Cruise Lines Operations Manual nor the
shipboard policies identified which “Authorized Personnel" were permitted access to the
stern. As a result, there was confusion onboard with regard to rightful access. When the
vessel underwent its cosmetic paddlewheel installation, the Coast Guard and vessel
representatives agreed that only engineers would have access to the stern in order to
service the hydraulic equipment. The only physical evidence attesting to this agreement
was the small red sign placed on the bulkhead leading back to the stern (albeit on the port
side only). No formal, written policy or list of designated personnel was ever created to
